cards.text: A Brussels rule on deforestation takes effect in December 2026. The hardest hit are not Malaysia's palm giants but its 450,000 smallholders.
cards.sub: Each plot must be mapped and proven clear of any forest cleared after 2020, paperwork a small farm struggles to produce.
sources: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 (EUDR; 31 Dec 2020 cutoff, geolocation); MPOB (~450,000 smallholders)

cards.h: A smallholder on a few hectares must now map every plot and document its history back to 2020 to keep selling into Europe.
cards.s: Independent smallholders work about 27% of Malaysia's 5.7 million hectares of oil palm.
cards.d: A smallholder on a few hectares must now map every plot and document its history back to 2020 to keep selling into Europe. Independent smallholders work about 27% of Malaysia's 5.7 million hectares of oil palm.
sources: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 (plot geolocation, deforestation-free after 31 Dec 2020); MPOB (smallholders ~27% of 5.7M ha)

cards.h: The EU now takes a small slice of Malaysia's palm exports, under 2 billion euros of 24 billion in goods. The rule still matters because its standard is spreading.
cards.s: Comply for Europe and you comply for the buyers copying Europe; fail and you fall out of the premium tier.
cards.d: The EU now takes a small slice of Malaysia's palm exports, under 2 billion euros of 24 billion in goods. The rule still matters because its traceability standard is spreading. Comply for Europe and you comply for the buyers copying Europe; fail and you fall out of the premium tier.
sources: EU-Malaysia trade figures (palm-related exports under EUR 2B of EUR 24B total goods); EUDR as emerging global traceability norm

cards.h: Malaysia made its own standard, MSPO, mandatory in 2020. By December 2024 it covered 86.5% of planted area, and the EU recognised it as a route to compliance.
cards.s: Yet about a quarter of licensed independent smallholders were still uncertified, the group most exposed to the deadline.
cards.d: Malaysia made its own standard, MSPO, mandatory in 2020. By December 2024 it covered 86.5% of planted area, and the EU recognised it as a route to compliance. Yet about a quarter of licensed independent smallholders were still uncertified, the group most exposed to the deadline.
sources: MPOB/MSPO (mandatory 2020; 86.5% of area / 4.89M ha by Dec 2024; 76.9% of 210,891 independent smallholders certified); EU-Malaysia joint press statement (MSPO recognition)

cards.text: The fight was sold as Europe versus Malaysia's sovereignty. The real divide runs inside Malaysia: the estate that can prove its provenance, and the smallholder who cannot.
It is like a new rule that every fish sold must name the boat that caught it. The trawler has the logbook; the man with one net does not.

Cleaner supply chains are a fair demand. Whether they lift the world's standards or just price out the smallest farmers depends on who pays for the paperwork, and so far it is the people least able to.

sources: Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 (EUDR) + amending regulation on application dates; European Commission EUDR pages; EU-Malaysia Joint Press Statement (EEAS); MPOB statistics; MSPO/MPOCC certification data; CSIS analysis; Pulitzer Center/Inside Climate News; ukragroconsult; ofimagazine. See engine/briefs/eudr-palm-oil-smallholders.md.
confidence: Medium-high on the deadlines (30 Dec 2026 large/medium; 30 June 2027 micro/small; cutoff 31 Dec 2020), the smallholder share (~27% of 5.7M ha), and MSPO coverage (86.5% by Dec 2024). Medium on the EU trade-value figure, where two sources disagree (< EUR 2B palm-related vs US$6.6B 'structured market'); the cards use the conservative 'small slice' framing and assert no single hard number.

source_notes: CONTRADICTION on EU palm trade value: one source gives palm-related exports to the EU as under EUR 2 billion (of EUR 24 billion total Malaysian goods to the EU); another calls the EU the 'single largest structured market for palm oil ... US$6.6 billion in 2023'. Likely different baskets/definitions. The cards avoid a single figure and say 'a small slice', which both sources support relative to India/China. Framing deliberately avoids both the 'EU discrimination' line and the 'Malaysia destroys forests' line; it is a burden-distribution and precedent story.
